name: Classic Mayan
confidence_why: Gronemeyer 2014, the only phonological study of Classic Mayan to take up the question, states that stress is not recoverable from the hieroglyphic script and has never been reconstructed, offering final stress only as an unsupported analogy with modern Ch'olan, while Macri 1988, Law 2006 and Bricker 2008 say nothing about stress and Kettunen and Helmke 2019 give final stress only as a pronunciation convention for Maya words in general.
catalog_citation: Gronemeyer, Sven. 2014. The Orthographic Conventions of Maya Hieroglyphic Writing: Being a Contribution to the Phonemic Reconstruction of Classic Mayan. PhD thesis, La Trobe University (Bundoora). 738 pp. doi:10.26181/21852843.v1 (OPAL open repository).

catalog_quote: [p.230 fn.525] Stress is in most instances put on the last syllable (cf. Fought [1967: 101] for CHR, Fox [1978: 37-46] for pM, Knowles [1984: 62] for CHN, Schumann Gálvez [1971: 35] for ITZ, [1997: 54-55] and MOP). [p.230] The present hypothesis sketch is just based on a handful of epigraphic examples and is by no means backed up by specific linguistic evidence for each form. [p.231] The answer whether stress was indicated is also difficult to pursue in the present thesis. ... More importantly, rather than by epigraphic evidence, ClM stress patterns require backwards reconstruction by historical linguistics, which has never been done before. [p.428] As section 3d in Chapter 3.2.2 outlined, stress is regularly put on the last syllable [sic] Ch’olan languages. [p.480] We again face the problem that ClM phonotactics are unknown and the data for modern Ch’olan languages are also not comprehensive. ... If there is a general tendency towards a final syllable stress, then several phenomena in relation to the suffix domain become explainable in an educated guess.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Classic (hieroglyphic) Mayan is not attested by the script and has never been reconstructed; the author's working assumption, by analogy with the modern Ch'olan daughter languages (Ch'ol, Chontal, Ch'orti') and proto-Mayan, is word-final primary stress, shifting onto suffixes in inflected/derived forms.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Hypothesised secondary stress two syllables before the final stressed syllable in trisyllabic+ forms (e.g. *[ʔu.ˌwa.jɪ.ˈbil], *[ˌjah.nə.ˈb'il], p.428; *[ˌʔu.tɪm.ˈxel], p.480) — explicitly speculative.
new_statements.exceptions: Author notes that in Chontal (Knowles 1984) and Ch'orti' (Fought 1967) lexical/root stress can dominate and stress may shift to suffixes or an ergative prefix, so some Classic Mayan forms might have retained root stress (pp.230 fn.526, 480); whether syn-/disharmonic spellings encode stress is left open ('The present hypothesis sketch is just based on a handful of epigraphic examples', p.230; 'ClM phonotactics are unknown', p.480).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (root vs. inflected word); statements are reconstructive assumptions for a written-only language, not observations; Kettunen & Helmke 2019:7,137 independently state the epigraphers' pronunciation convention that Maya words are stressed on the last syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Gronemeyer's 'Classic Mayan (ClM)' = the language of the Classic-period hieroglyphic inscriptions = Glottolog epig1241 'Epigraphic Mayan' (ISO emy; often called Classic Ch'olti'an). His stress assumption is imported from the modern Ch'olan daughters Ch'ol (chol1282), Chontal de Tabasco (taba1266) and Ch'orti' (chor1273) and from proto-Mayan (Fox 1978); it is a reconstruction, not an attested property. Kettunen & Helmke's statement concerns the conventional pronunciation of 'Maya words' by epigraphers, not Classic Mayan specifically.

sources.note: Ch.3.2.2 sec.3d 'Syllable weight and stress' (pp.229-231, fn.525-526), p.428, p.480: Classic Mayan (ClM) stress is not recoverable from the script ('ClM stress patterns require backwards reconstruction by historical linguistics, which has never been done before', p.231; 'ClM phonotactics are unknown', p.480); as a working assumption stress is taken to fall on the last syllable as in modern Ch'olan (fn.525 p.230; p.428), with hypothesised secondary stress two syllables before the final (p.428); discusses whether syn-/disharmonic spellings could encode stress but leaves it open.
